blocks.text: Before getting into operations and patterns, let's understand what a matrix actually is and why it exists.
You already know what an array is a list of elements in a single line:

blocks.alt: 1D array: a list of elements in a single line

blocks.text: But what if your data is naturally two dimensional? Like a seating chart, a spreadsheet, a game board, or an image?
A single array can't represent that cleanly. You need rows and columns. That is exactly what a matrix is.
A matrix is simply a 2D array an array of arrays. Each element lives at a specific row and column.
3 rows, 4 columns:
2. How Elements are Stored
Every element has an address a row index and a column index. You always say row first, then column.
Matrix (2D Array) Basics
A matrix is a 2D array organized into rows and columns. In programming, it is represented as an array of arrays, where the first index selects the row and the second index selects the column.
The dimensions of a matrix are written as m × n, where m is the number of rows and n is the number of columns.
In the example above, the matrix is 3 × 4.
Rows run horizontally from left to right, while columns run vertically from top to bottom. Indexing is zero-based, which means the first row is row 0 and the first column is column 0.
So when you write matrix[1][2], you are selecting the element in the second row and third column, which is 7.

content.title: 3. Matrix as a Hidden Graph Structure

blocks.text: A matrix can be interpreted as a graph without explicitly storing edges. Each cell behaves like a node, and its connections are derived using position-based movement.

items:
Implicit Connectivity:
Instead of storing adjacency lists, neighbors of a cell (i, j) are calculated using directions (up, down, left, right), making the graph “implicit”.

Graph Algorithm Usage:
This structure allows direct application of traversal techniques like BFS and DFS for problems such as shortest paths, island counting, and region exploration.

Matrix Traversal Patterns
There are different ways to traverse a matrix. Each pattern is used for a different type of problem.
1. Linear Traversal
You visit every cell one by one.

Row-major means go left to right, then move to the next row.
Column-major means go top to bottom first.
Use this when you just need to check or process every cell.
2. Diagonal Traversal
You move along diagonals instead of rows or columns.
Here you start from different diagonal starting points and move in a diagonal direction.
Use this when the problem involves diagonals.
3. Spiral Traversal
You traverse layer by layer from outside to inside.
You move right → down → left → up, and keep shrinking the boundaries.
Use this when the problem asks for spiral order.

content.title: 6. Types of Matrices You Will Encounter

blocks.text: Understanding matrix types helps you quickly identify what kind of operations a problem might need.

• Square Matrix (rows = columns)
A square matrix has the same number of rows and columns (like 3×3, 4×4). These are very common in problems involving rotation, transpose, and diagonal traversal. Most grid-based problems use square matrices because they allow symmetric operations.

• Row Matrix (single row)
A row matrix has only one row (1×N). It behaves exactly like a normal array. You can only move left or right, so problems on this are usually simple and similar to 1D array problems.

• Column Matrix (single column)
A column matrix has only one column (N×1). It is like a vertical array. You process it from top to bottom, and it behaves similar to a 1D array but in vertical form.

• Identity Matrix (diagonal = 1, rest = 0)
In an identity matrix, all diagonal elements are 1 and all other elements are 0. It acts like a neutral element in matrix multiplication. It is commonly used in math, linear algebra, and transformations.

• Sparse Matrix (mostly zeros)
A sparse matrix has mostly 0 values and very few non-zero elements. Instead of storing the whole matrix, we store only non-zero values to save space and improve efficiency. It is commonly used in graphs and large data problems.
